questions.q: What does Baxter mean by a 'dysfunctional narrative'?
choices: A story about an unhappy family
A story told out of chronological order
A story whose protagonist is acted upon, with responsibility always located elsewhere
A story without a climax
questions.explain: The term describes how a story is built, not its subject matter.

questions.q: Why does Baxter begin with the phrase 'mistakes were made'?
choices: As an example of good dialogue
Because it admits error while hiding who made it
Because it's a famous first line
To illustrate the inverted pyramid
questions.explain: He sees the same evasion of agency spreading from public life into fiction.

questions.q: A workshop story's climax is a character finally telling her mother everything that was done to her years ago. What would Baxter ask?
choices: Where is her present-tense choice, and what does she get wrong and own?
Is the reversal also a recognition?
Is the inciting incident on page 12?
Does the scene turn a value?
questions.explain: Baxter worries when climaxes become accusations or recognitions of grievance rather than choices.

questions.q: What is Baxter's objection in 'Against Epiphanies'?
choices: That stories should end in death
That Joyce was a poor writer
That stories need a moral
That the sudden-insight ending has become a reflex, as if understanding were the same as change
questions.explain: He questions the unearned epiphany laid on in a final paragraph.

questions.q: Which statement best represents Baxter's position?
choices: Stories shouldn't be about victims
All protagonists should be heroic
Stories can be about terrible harm but should still give their people agency
Plot matters less than style
questions.explain: His target is a narrative habit that erases agency, not the subject of harm.

questions.q: Which later essay revived a related debate about stories built on past injury?
choices: 'The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction'
Parul Sehgal's 'The Case Against the Trauma Plot'
Poe's 'The Philosophy of Composition'
'Rhyming Action'
questions.explain: Sehgal's 2021 New Yorker essay made a related argument about trauma as an all-explaining backstory.

questions.q: What does Baxter value in characters instead of passivity?
choices: The interesting mistake: a choice they get wrong and then own
Unshakable virtue
Hidden supernatural powers
A single dominant emotion
questions.explain: Owning a mistake is how a character becomes someone.

ideas: A culture that says 'mistakes were made' produces stories in which nobody makes them.
Fiction comes alive when characters make mistakes and then have to own them.
The sudden flash of insight at a story's end has become a reflex that substitutes understanding for change.
